title: Inquest determines death was suicide
article: A coroner's jury has concluded Paul Horan's 2010 death was suicide, caused by a toxic level of an anti-depressant drug.
Horan died in OPP custody, after he was arrested on Hwy. 402 for failing to stop for police.
The jury's finding and four recommendations -- three of which apply to hospital emergency departments -- were based on evidence heard at a five-day Sarnia inquest that ended Wednesday.
Horan, a 43-year-old Sarnia man, died in the early morning on Sept. 24, 2010, at Bluewater Health's Charlotte Eleanor Englehart site in Petrolia, a few hours after his arrest.
He had been prescribed the anti-depressant, amitriptyline, and an empty prescription bottle was found along the highway after the arresting officer saw something thrown from Horan's vehicle.
Prescription records indicate there could have been more than 50 pills in the bottle when Horan was pulled over. The prescription called for him to take eight pills daily.
A Centre of Forensic Sciences analysis discovered a toxic level in Horan's blood and an autopsy revealed superficial injuries on his body, including bruising -- attributed to being handcuffed.
A toxic level in Horan's blood was discovered by an analysis done by the Centre of Forensic Sciences.
A cousin testified Horan was in a good mood when he left for his night shift job in Strathroy, Sept. 23, 2010.

In his final submission to the inquest, David Horan said his brother could not handle pressure and could have panicked and ingested some pills when he saw the emergency lights of the OPP cruiser behind him.

He said maybe something could have been done if his brother had gotten to the hospital sooner. An OPP officer requested an ambulance at 12:09 a.m. -- when Horan was unresponsive but breathing. He arrived at the hospital at 12:52 a.m.
A time analysis presented to jurors indicated paramedics were treating Horan when he still would have been 10 minutes away from the hospital if the officer had decided to drive him instead.
Attempts to resuscitate Horan at the hospital failed and he died at 2:20 a.m.
One of the jury's recommendations is emergency departments should have a policy requiring staff to contact the Poison Control Centre when treating a patient overdosing on an unknown substance.
A phone number for the centre was prominently displayed near a phone at the Petrolia hospital's emergency department, but the centre was not contacted by staff.
Horan was still breathing when he arrived at the hospital, but his blood pressure was low.
According to a paramedic's assessment, Horan's state of unconsciousness was three on a scale where a conscious, healthy person is 15.
His eyes were not reacting to light.
Jurors recommended emergency departments consider having intralipids -- a fat emulsion that can inhibit the absorption of anti-depressants during an overdose -- available to treat patients.

Doctor groups like the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario should also review whether emergency room doctors need to have current certifications in Advanced Cardiac Life Support and Advanced Trauma Life Support, jurors said.
The doctor treating Horan had those certifications.
Fourth, jurors said all methadone clinics should require patients to report any admission or attendance at a hospital for mental health issues.

Horan had been prescribed methadone for a past addiction to painkillers and was entitled to possess six daily doses, known as carries. He'd been admitted to hospital for a mental health assessment following a blood-pressure medication overdose in 2009.
That resulted in a temporary suspension of his carry privileges. Those were reinstated months later.
His methadone clinic doctor determined Horan was optimistic about his future shortly before his death.
Recommendations from coroner's juries are seriously considered by authorities and have made Ontario a safer place, said coroner's counsel Randy Evans before jurors began their deliberations.
